title: Replace a worn gravity-conveyor roller: retract its spring-loaded hex axle and seat a new one in the hex holes
instruction: Replace the worn roller with the new one, and put the worn roller in the reject tray.
context: Gravity roller conveyors carry cartons and totes across factories, packaging lines, loading docks, warehouses and fulfillment centers, where maintenance and floor crews swap worn or seized pop-out rollers in place by hand with no tools: General Maintenance and Repair Workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, 1.5M US workers: 'Dismantle machines, equipment, or devices to access and remove defective parts'), Industrial Machinery Mechanics and Maintenance Workers (49-9041.00 / 49-9043.00, 495k US workers: 'Repair or replace broken or malfunctioning components'), and Hand Laborers and Material Movers (53-7062.00, 3.0M US workers), with 618,000 maintenance mechanics in manufacturing, warehousing, wholesale and courier sites alone (BLS OEWS). Unlike a round spring spindle, a conveyor roller has a non-round 7/16 in hex axle (11.1 mm AF) inside a free-spinning steel tube that must register within 8 deg of closed 11.9 mm AF hex holes while one hand holds the stub drawn in against its 13.6 N spring.
setup: An installed light-duty gravity roller conveyor section, bolted down on the table, running away from the robot: two blue 12 ga (2.7 mm) steel angle rails, webs 63.5 mm tall, 381 mm apart (15 in between frames), 610 mm long, from 0.129 to 0.739 m in front of the arm bases, centred on their midline; in each web five 7/16 in hex holes (11.9 mm across flats, flats top and bottom) 44.5 mm above the table on 114.3 mm centres. Five rollers in the holes: galvanized steel tube 48.3 mm across, 368.3 mm long, 1.16 kg, on a spring-retained 7/16 in hex steel axle (11.1 mm across flats, 419.1 mm long, 25.4 mm past each tube end; slides 16 mm toward the roller's left end against a spring, 4 N rising to 13.6 N). The second from the robot (0.30 m) is worn: rust-stained, a scored band, a red paint mark near its left end. To the right: a blue plastic tray (466 x 86 mm, 25 mm walls, centre 0.33 m forward, 0.30 m right) holding the new roller lying along the table, left end away from the robot; a grey reject tray, same size, empty, centre 0.33 m forward, 0.42 m right.
scoring: At the end. Worn roller in the reject tray: its tube's middle inside the tray's walls, resting on its floor. A new-roller axle end is seated when the axle passes through the empty slot's hex hole (within 3 mm of its centre) and its end sticks out at least 5 mm past that rail's outer face. 1.0: worn roller in the reject tray and both new-roller ends seated; 0.5: worn roller in the tray and one end seated; 0.25: worn roller in the tray; 0 otherwise. Real trial: photo of the tray; at each rail, a ruler on the outer face shows the axle end through the hole.
reset_notes: Refit the worn roller in the second position from the robot (its red paint mark to the robot's left), lay the new roller back in the blue tray (its left end away from the robot, a hex corner turned 15 degrees from straight up), empty the reject tray. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: PhysX at 240 Hz. Each roller is an articulation: tube, free bearings (seal drag holds the axle's turn below 0.017 N m), axle on a 16 mm spring slide (600 N/m, 4 N preload). The rails' hex holes are real openings; the four other rollers are fixed and do not spin. Friction: steel 0.3, trays 0.4.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (4,500 steps; left arm grasped the worn roller's tube but never retracted the spring axle, so the roller stayed locked in the rails); scripted demo: 1.0 (success at step 2,410). README checks (CPU): one end seated 0.5; worn roller out only 0.25; no motion 0.
